chief_complaint: chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and hemoptysis
hpi_details: A 50-year-old female presents to the clinic with chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and hemoptysis. The patient states the symptoms started about 6 weeks ago and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks she has developed lung cancer because she is coughing up blood and shedding weight without trying.
concerns: She is worried she will need debilitating chemotherapy and will no longer be able to financially support or care for her family.
expectations: She hopes to get an urgent chest CT scan today and some strong medicine to halt the coughing and bleeding.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Airborne isolation, RIPE therapy, report to public health, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and hemoptysis

Key HPI features: A 50-year-old female presents to the clinic with chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and hemoptysis. The patient states the symptoms started about 6 weeks ago and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 38.1C (low-grade), HR 92, BP 108/68, weight down 6kg over 2 months. Cachectic appearance, post-tussive crackles in the right upper lobe. Sputum AFB smear positive; chest X-ray shows right upper lobe cavitary infiltrate.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Lung cancer without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Significant hemoptysis.
management_principles: Plan for Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Airborne isolation, RIPE therapy, report to public health
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and hemoptysis

A 50-year-old female presents to the clinic with chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and hemoptysis. The patient states the symptoms started about 6 weeks ago and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 38.1C (low-grade), HR 92, BP 108/68, weight down 6kg over 2 months. Cachectic appearance, post-tussive crackles in the right upper lobe. Sputum AFB smear positive; chest X-ray shows right upper lobe cavitary infiltrate.
reference_soap.assessment: Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis, sputum AFB smear-positive with right upper lobe cavitary disease on chest imaging.
reference_soap.plan: Plan for Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis: Airborne isolation, RIPE therapy, report to public health. Consult specialist if symptoms worsen. Counsel patient.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis
Implement evidence-based management plan: Airborne isolation, RIPE therapy, report to public health

teaching.one_liner: Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection of the lungs causing chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and hemoptysis — requires airborne isolation and multi-drug (RIPE) therapy.

must_ask.say: How many weeks or months have you had this cough?
Have you had night sweats, fever, or weight loss?
Have you coughed up any blood?
Have you been around anyone with tuberculosis, or traveled to a high-risk area?
Do you live in crowded conditions?

history.answer: I've been coughing up blood lately, and I've lost quite a bit of weight without trying.
The blood definitely comes up when I cough from deep in my chest, not from throwing up or running down my throat.
It's about a teaspoon or two of blood mixed into my phlegm a few times a day, not large mouthfuls.
It is bright red streaks mixed with phlegm, and there is no food or dark coffee-ground material in it.
I first noticed the blood in my phlegm about a week ago, and it has happened almost every day since.
The cough actually started about six weeks ago and has been steadily getting worse over time.
I cough up a modest amount of yellowish phlegm every morning, but it doesn't smell foul or come up in huge cupfuls.
I've had a low fever and mild chills on and off, especially in the late afternoons and evenings.
I wake up drenched in sweat almost every night, and I've been feeling completely worn out.
I've lost about six kilograms over the last two months without changing my diet, and my clothes are very loose.
I feel slightly winded when climbing stairs, but I haven't had sudden breathlessness or sharp chest pain.
history.topic: Shortness of breath and chest pain

history.answer: Neither of my legs is swollen or painful, and I haven't had recent surgery, prolonged bed rest, or long trips.
I can lie flat comfortably at night, and I don't wake up choking or gasping for air.
No, I haven't had any nosebleeds, nasal scabs, or sinus headaches.
My urine looks normal light yellow, never dark or cola-colored, and my output has been regular.
No, I haven't had any unusual skin bruises, bleeding gums, or blood in my stool.
I haven't had any stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, heartburn, or black tarry stools.
A coworker sharing my office was diagnosed with active pulmonary tuberculosis about four months ago.
I haven't traveled overseas recently, and I have never lived in a shelter or correctional facility.
I thought maybe I have lung cancer, since I've been coughing up blood and losing weight so fast without even trying.
I'm terrified that I might need chemotherapy and won't be able to work and take care of my family.
I was hoping to get an urgent chest scan today and some medicine that will stop this coughing and bleeding right away.
I have always been healthy, with no history of asthma, pneumonia, high blood pressure, or diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I don't take any prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink a glass of wine socially once or twice a month, and I don't use recreational drugs.
I work as an office clerk, and I live in an apartment with my husband and grown daughter.
Nobody in my family has had lung disease, tuberculosis, bleeding disorders, or cancer.
My last period started three weeks ago and my cycle has been somewhat irregular lately, but there is no chance of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Patient appears thin, fatigued, and mildly cachectic, but is in no acute respiratory distress.
Blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, pulse 92 beats/min, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 38.1°C, oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
Nasal mucosa and oral cavity are clear, with no active bleeding, mucosal ulcers, or blood crusting.
No palpable cervical, supraclavicular, or axillary lymphadenopathy.
Dullness to percussion over the right upper posterior chest; resonant throughout all other lung fields.
Post-tussive crackles auscultated over the right upper lung field; normal vesicular breath sounds without wheezing elsewhere.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs heard.
Jugular venous pressure is normal with no visible jugular venous distension.
No digital clubbing, cyanosis, or peripheral edema noted in either extremity.
Both calves are supple, non-tender, and symmetric in girth with no signs of deep vein thrombosis.
